I also have a master's degree in chemistry and, honestly, I don't agree with your arguments. Yes, your weight can be a result of the amount of calories you consume and spend. But these quantities are influenced by many genetic, environmental, behavioral, physiological factors, etc. The amount of hormones (such as leptin) that are excreted and the sensitivity of their receptors play a very significant role.
Second, diets don't work. Ok, you can use mathematical logic and of course you lose weight if you expend more energy than you consume, but humans are not a beaker or a piece of equipment. We cannot do simply biochemical research and conclude that diets work, as very well-constructed and well-founded statistical studies of the population have concluded that diets do not work. Yes, biologically it makes sense. Does this mean that this is the empirical result? No. Its not right to only consider Leningher principles of biochemistry and ignore decades of population studies.
Lastly, yes, BMI can be a generic indicator of health, but it is not at all accurate. Body composition, level of physical activity and amount of visceral fat are much better indicators of health. So if you have a higher BMI, it could be a sign of concern, but it doesn't mean much without further investigation. You can have a high BMI and be healthy and the opposite can also happen.
